# Results — Study 149 (Daylight-Saving) on real ^GSPC daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py).  The claim: the Monday
after a US DST clock change (spring-forward or fall-back) earns abnormally negative
returns, attributed to sleep disruption (Kamstra, Kramer & Levi 2000).  We test
post-DST Mondays vs all other Mondays on ^GSPC daily close-to-close returns
(1980-01-03 to 2026-06-12) and pin the gap against a random-Monday placebo.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC (Yahoo Finance) | 1980-01-03 to 2026-06-12 | 11,706 daily returns | `3ad46b2324e0` |
| DST Mondays (spring + fall) | 1980-2026 | 93 events | calendar rule (no download) |
| Other Mondays | same window | 2,119 | — |

As-of 2026-06-14. Reproduce with `python examples/verify.py --fetch`.

## The headline test — post-DST Monday vs other Mondays

| Arm | n | mean (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **Post-DST Monday** | 93 | **−17.69** | **−1.20** |
| Other Mondays (control) | 2,119 | +2.21 | +0.88 |
| **Difference** | — | **−19.89** | **Welch *t* = −1.19** |

- The post-DST Monday underperforms other Mondays by **−19.89 bps** on average.
- The Welch *t* on this difference is **−1.19** — below the |*t*| ≥ 2 inference bar.
  The result is **statistically indistinguishable from noise** over 93 events.
- The HAC *t* on the DST arm alone is −1.20: the DST mean is negative but with
  a standard error too wide to call.

## Placebo — random Monday relabelling (500 seeds)

| | bps |
|---|--:|
| Observed gap | −19.89 |
| Placebo mean | +0.03 |
| Placebo std | 14.33 |
| One-sided p-value (gap ≤ null) | 0.084 |

The observed gap sits in the left tail of the placebo distribution (about 8th
percentile), but the 5% threshold is not cleared: **p = 0.084**, not significant
by conventional standards.  With only 93 DST observations the study is extremely
low-power, and the gap's sign is consistent with the original claim — but
consistent-with is not the same as confirmed.

## Season split — spring-forward vs fall-back

| Season | n | mean (bps/day) | Welch *t* vs other |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Spring-forward (lose 1h sleep) | 47 | −18.95 | −1.03 |
| Fall-back (gain 1h sleep) | 46 | −16.40 | −0.70 |
| Other Mondays | 2,119 | +2.21 | — |

Both seasons are negative, but neither approaches significance.  Kamstra et al.'s
prediction that spring-forward > fall-back in magnitude holds directionally
(−18.95 vs −16.40 bps), but the difference is negligible and both are noise.

## Era split — pre-2000 vs post-2000

| Era | n (DST) | gap (bps) | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Pre-2000 (in-sample for KKL) | ~40 | −35.68 | −1.19 |
| Post-2000 (out-of-sample) | ~53 | −7.98 | −0.42 |

The gap is roughly 4x larger in the era the original paper covered, and is small
and noisy post-2000.  This is consistent with either (a) the effect always being
noise and the original result being a lucky draw, or (b) a real effect that has
decayed substantially since publication and awareness — we cannot tell from 93
events either way.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.**  Welch *t* = −1.19 on the headline gap; HAC *t* = −1.20 on
  the DST arm alone; placebo p = 0.084.  No result clears the |*t*| ≥ 2 bar.
  The negative gap directionally matches the original claim but is statistically
  indistinguishable from the Monday-return noise band.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.**  With only 2 events per year and a gap that is not
  significantly different from zero, there is nothing to trade.  Even if the
  effect were real at −20 bps, two trades per year generate essentially zero
  annualised alpha relative to the strategy's basis risk.
- **Contested / fragile (3rd axis).**  Pinegar (2002) showed the KKL result
  vanishes with minor methodological changes; our out-of-sample (post-2000)
  confirms fragility (t = −0.42).  This is a textbook example of an isolated,
  low-power calendar anomaly that rests on a small-sample effect that does not
  survive.
